items.abstract_or_text: Site-selective bridging of cysteines and native disulfide bonds represents a powerful strategy for peptide and protein modification. However, most bis-electrophilic reagents rely on azide-alkyne cycloadditions for downstream bioconjugation, while existing tetrazine-based cysteine linkers can generate undesired byproducts, such as peptide cyclodimers, or incorporate additional components that are not directly involved in conjugation or ligation. Here, we report divinyl- s -tetrazine ( DvTz ) as a minimal linchpin in which the electron-deficient tetrazine core activates the vinyl groups as Michael acceptors for efficient cysteine conjugation, while simultaneously serving as a bioorthogonal handle for subsequent inverse-electron-demand Diels-Alder (IEDDA) ligation. DvTz enables high-yielding, cysteine-selective stapling of unprotected peptides, tolerates all twenty canonical amino acids, and accommodates a broad range of sequences and stapling distances. A one-pot stapling-IEDDA sequence enables facile installation of functional tags without intermediate purification. The chemistry was extended to antibody Fab fragments, achieving site-specific disulfide rebridging and subsequent IEDDA ligation across three distinct Fab proteins, with exclusive formation of singly conjugated species. A Fab-drug conjugate was constructed with retained antigen-binding activity and selective potency against HER2-positive cell lines, showcasing the application of DvTz in therapeutically relevant settings. Collectively, this work establishes DvTz as a simple and versatile linchpin for peptide and protein bioconjugation.

items.title: Robot-Accelerated Perovskite Investigation and Discovery: Copper Halide Perovskitoids
items.abstract_or_text: Metal halide perovskitoids are a compositionally and structurally diverse class of materials with many applications. High-throughput experimentation is a valuable tool for exploratory synthesis of these materials, particularly as part of the search for environmentally friendly lead-free perovskitoids. Herein, we describe an automated, high-throughput approach for metal halide perovskite single crystal discovery based on antisolvent vapor diffusion (ASVD) to rapidly identify and optimize synthesis conditions for the formation of high-quality single crystals. Using this automated approach, a total of 315 copper iodide/chloride perovskite synthesis reactions were conducted using five organoammonium cations, resulting in nine new phases. items.title: Integrating stool chemistry measurements with metagenomics in adults reveals distinct gut health profiles
items.abstract_or_text: Stool chemistry metrics, including calprotectin, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA, are used to assess gut inflammation in clinical or research settings. However, these measures in isolation provide a limited view of gut physiology and lack microbial context. Shotgun metagenomics offers a comprehensive assessment of the gut microbiome's taxonomic composition and functional potential, yet its integration with stool chemistry metrics remains underexplored. We analyzed 877 adult stool samples with paired shotgun metagenomic sequencing and chemistry measurements to integrate the microbiome with 12 stool chemistry metrics. Calprotectin, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA were associated with shifts in microbiome composition (beta diversity), while deviations from typical levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including butyrate, were associated with both changes in alpha diversity and microbiome composition. Network analysis revealed two distinct microbial neighborhoods: one associated with higher butyrate and lower calprotectin and lactoferrin and another associated with lower butyrate and higher calprotectin and lactoferrin. Machine learning models trained on taxonomic and functional data showed modest discrimination of stool chemistry states, performing best for SCFA deficiency and less well for host-derived inflammatory metrics. Together, these findings systematically characterize microbiome-stool chemistry relationships across a large paired dataset, providing a framework for interpreting stool chemistry metrics in the context of shotgun metagenomic profiles.

items.title: MutQA: A Cross-Validated Q&A Dataset for Genetic Mutations
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce MutQA, a dataset of 330,387 citation-grounded question-answer (QA) pairs linking genetic mutations to their functional consequences as described in the biomedical literature. Each record pairs a protein-coding mutation with a natural-language question and an evidence-backed answer anchored to sentences in one of 27,442 open-access PubMed Central articles, spanning 6,620 genes and 125,593 gene-variant pairs. The dataset is constructed using CrossValQA, a framework that enforces information isolation between independent LLMs: one model generates QA pairs from an article, a second model answers the same question without access to the first model's response, and a third model judges whether each model's rationale supports the other's answer, so that retained QA pairs are reproducible from the source text rather than hallucinated. Of 401,406 audited QA pairs, 82.7% pass both directions of this cross-validation; those with a recoverable reference protein sequence form the released benchmark. In a 999-pair stratified audit, two expert annotators agree exactly on 86.4% of cross-validated QA pairs (95% CI 83.7-89.0; n = 638), a tier in which about 90% of ratings are "correct". Individual LLM judges agree with individual annotators at a comparable 87.0% on this tier but far less on QA pairs that fail cross-validation. Fine-tuning MutaPLM on MutQA nearly doubles its mean LLM-judge score for question-conditioned mutation-effect answering (1.45 to 2.82 on a 0-5 scale) and improves mutation-recovery accuracy from effect descriptions from 19.4% to 32.1%. Providing variant-matched MutQA retrieval context, without fine-tuning, improves strict answer accuracy across four LLM families by 20.0-28.6 percentage points, demonstrating the framework's ability to improve the reliability of LLM answers. We also apply CrossValQA to proteomics, providing a proof of concept for its use beyond mutation-specific QA. We release the dataset, construction framework, and evaluation code.

items.title: Framework-Templated Single Clathrate Hydrate Cages in Metal–Organic Frameworks
items.abstract_or_text: Molecular simulations identify metal–organic framework (MOF) pores that retain single methane hydrate cages and, for a nonstandard 16-water cage, support its assembly from disordered water. In smooth spherical pores, a methane molecule assembled twenty waters into the pentagonal dodecahedron of structure I hydrate and sixteen waters into a 435661 cage, a polyhedron that no known hydrate crystal contains. These idealized models were built by language-model agents and then walked back toward real materials, an approach referred to here as agentic doodling, and they guided a screening of 120,419 experimental MOF structures. Most size-matched pores pulled the cage apart, but a small set of frameworks kept it intact at 216 K, better with methane than without, and ELOZIQ kept the dodecahedron up to 270 K, near the melting temperature of the water model. In XODDED and GUQMAH, the nonstandard cage was held at least as well as in an ideal spherical pore, and it self-assembled around methane from randomly placed water, with nearly all of its edges hydrogen bonded. The pores template the cages through a moderate attraction spread over the cage corners rather than through strong binding sites placed at the corners. These results open a route to designing MOFs that hold single hydrate cages, including cages that do not occur in bulk hydrates.

items.title: Binning-based Methods for Model Fitting and Data Splitting Improve Machine Learning Imbalanced Regression
items.abstract_or_text: Modelling quantitative genomics data remains challenging due to imbalanced target distributions, non-independent observations, and substantial computational costs. This study examines the challenges and current methods, proposes new methods, applies these methods across two case studies: a controlled setting with synthetically generated data and on real genomics datasets. Effective modelling of imbalanced data starts with density estimation. Density estimation via binning facilitates downstream analytical steps. Minimum Transformation Binning is a novel method that improves current binning methods for density estimation. Data splitting of imbalanced and non-independent observations is best accomplished by objective data splitting which entails randomly generating splits, scoring them, and selecting the best scoring one. This study conducts an empirical comparison of scoring functions toward an optimal objective data splitting method, finding the use of all-against-one absolute relative difference to be the best scoring function. Model fitting methods can be divided into loss functions and data balancing. Two methods have been previously proposed based on weighting error functions by the reciprocal or complement of the density estimation. This study conducts a comparison of these methods on the case studies, finding that reciprocal density weighting significantly outperforms non-weighted and complement density weighting. This study also tests model fitting with reciprocal weighted sampling per epoch for imbalanced regression. While this method does not generally improve performance, it uses significantly less resources in model fitting which can be beneficial for hyperparameter optimization. Together, this study provides a unified framework for effective modelling of imbalanced regression, especially imbalanced genomics data.

items.title: Coverage Under Contradiction: A Benchmark for Negation-Aware Retrieval
items.abstract_or_text: Coverage-evaluation benchmarks quantify whether retrieved evidence covers the different pieces of information needed to satisfy an information need. Existing benchmarks mostly consider factual claims that may already be known to pretrained retrieval components, leaving open whether retrievers find corpus evidence when it contradicts those priors. We study how retrievers behave when their parametric knowledge and the information in a corpus disagree. To do so, we develop a process to augment a nugget-based coverage benchmark with controlled contradictions. For each nugget, we create a negated counterpart and edit its supporting documents to support that negation while preserving the context. Applying this process to CoverageBench, a benchmark measuring information coverage, we create CoverageBench-Negate, spanning six datasets and roughly 63,000 original-edited evidence pairs (one per nugget-document link). We attach rich construction metadata to every pair and additionally provide out-of-family LLM judgments over all pairs and a human audit of a sample. In baseline experiments, BM25 separates original from edited near-twin evidence substantially better than dense retrievers (Qwen3 and Jina), which stay near chance. We release the benchmark on Hugging Face Datasets (nuggets, documents, pairs) together with the construction materials, including the prompts used to create it.

items.title: Neuronal Identity as an Organizational Basis for Analyzing Neural Population Dynamics
items.abstract_or_text: Individual neurons exhibit diverse molecular, morphological, and electrophysiological properties that shape their distinct roles in neural circuits. While these multimodal features are largely shared across individuals, they remain an underutilized source of information in analyzing neural population dynamics. We posit that these shared biological profiles provide a common reference for relating neural dynamics across subjects and recording sessions. Our framework leverages this structure by routing neurons into latent groups based on their biological profiles and analyzing population dynamics through group-level representations. Because these assignments are anchored in biological properties that are consistent across subjects, the learned organization supports transfer to unseen animals without retraining or neuron-wise correspondence. We evaluate our framework on whole-brain calcium imaging in larval zebrafish and large-scale electrophysiology in the mouse visual cortex. Across both species and recording modalities, the framework delivers state-of-the-art performance in both neural decoding and manifold analysis: it achieves superior decoding of behavior and stimulus labels while better preserving the temporal consistency and local geometric structure of latent trajectories on unseen data. Our experiments demonstrate that not only does providing biological features improve baseline performance, but our proposed framework achieves even stronger results by using these properties to explicitly structure the population rather than treating them as auxiliary inputs. Together, these results suggest that organizing neural populations by their multimodal biological features offers a promising framework for generalizing population dynamics across subjects and recording sessions.

items.title: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Modern language models are trained on far more language than children experience, but we know much less about learning from small, naturalistic datasets. We train small GPT-2 models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (BabyView) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (TinyDialogues), varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data. Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. Much of this specialization is lexical and distributional: a simple 5-gram model reproduces the cross-child pattern (r=.91). Training on data from multiple children clearly improves prediction of pooled held-out language relative to training on a single child's input without a similarly clear improvement on grammatical benchmarks. Across data sizes, naturalistic and synthetic training inputs also produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, with important differences between grammatical phenomena. Together, these results show that small-data language learning depends not only on how much language a model sees, but on which environments it comes from and how well that input matches what the model is asked to predict.

items.title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization
items.abstract_or_text: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.

items.title: Molecular basis of competence for neural induction in the chick embryo
items.abstract_or_text: Competence is the capacity of a cell or tissue to respond to a specific inducing signal from a neighbouring tissue, by changing its fate in a specific direction. Neural induction is the process by which the epiblast of the early embryo responds to signals from the organizer (the tip of the primitive streak in amniotes) by forming a neural plate. Here we study why three regions of the early chick embryo lack competence to respond to neural induction by a grafted organizer: the outer anterior area opaca and the posterior area opaca at primitive streak stages (HH3+-4-), and the inner anterior area opaca at head process stage (HH5), in comparison with the competent anterior inner area opaca at HH3+-4-. Molecular analysis of these tissues, and their temporal dynamics following exposure to the organizer, reveals several differences. Among them, increased BMP and decreased ERK signalling characterise the non-competent regions. Inhibition of BMP can restore competence to HH5 epiblast; a combination of BMP-inhibition with ERK-stimulation by FGF8 can confer competence to the outer area opaca, whereas none of these can endow posterior epiblast with competence for neural induction. We conclude that spatiotemporal competence of epiblast for neural induction is regulated by several mechanisms, including extracellular signals.

items.title: A vagal-to-sympathetic reflex controls lung vascular leak
items.abstract_or_text: Dynamic regulation of the vascular barrier is required for an effective inflammatory response, allowing delivery of plasma proteins and immune cells to sites of insult. Although normally protective, sustained leak becomes costly in organs like the lung, where swelling stiffens tissue and impairs breathing, yet many upstream regulators remain unidentified. Using a chemogenetic screen of vagal afferent subtypes, we identify a neural reflex that drives lung vascular leak. The reflex originates in an orphan population of neurons expressing Cysltr2 that innervates alveolar capillary beds and senses both mechanical and inflammatory stimuli, fitting classic definitions of pulmonary 'J' receptors, an afferent subtype described anatomically since the 1950s whose function has remained speculative. Activating CYSLTR2 neurons increases lung vascular leak within minutes and causes perivascular edema and respiratory dysfunction, whereas silencing them during inhaled allergen challenge reduces leak and improves lung mechanics. Rather than acting locally through antidromic peptide release, this reflex engages brainstem relays and sympathetic efferents to broadcast its effects throughout lung vasculature. Vagal control of the vascular barrier thus forms an axis of organ defense that can go awry in disease, revealing new ways to regulate organ fluid balance upstream of the endothelium
